lessons.title: The Mysterious Balloon: What Invisible Force Is at Work?

quiz.prompt: A group rubs a dry balloon on one learner's hair 20 times and then slowly pulls it away. Which statement best describes what they observed?
choices: The hair rises and follows the balloon, even though nothing visible connects them.
The hair is pushed away from the balloon.
The hair stays attached to the balloon only because of glue-like stickiness.
The hair stays flat unless the balloon touches it.
quiz.rationale: The observation was that hair strands rise and follow the balloon, up to about 5 cm away, without any visible link. This describes what was seen and does not explain it.
quiz.placement: Station 1, Hair: 20 strokes of the balloon on dry hair

quiz.prompt: After testing a rubbed balloon on hair, the wall and paper, a group also tries an unrubbed balloon on the same things. Why do they do this?
choices: To find out whether the balloon is magnetic.
To show that the effects are linked to rubbing, because the unrubbed balloon does nothing.
To check which colour of balloon works best.
To save the rubbed balloon so it lasts longer.
quiz.rationale: The unrubbed balloon is the control. It had no effect on hair, wall or paper, so the effects are linked to the rubbing.
quiz.placement: Control: an unrubbed balloon tried on hair, wall and paper

quiz.prompt: Two balloons are rubbed on hair and hung from separate threads. When they are brought near each other, they move apart. Which word do learners use to describe this pattern?
choices: Repel
No effect
Magnetise
Attract
quiz.rationale: Objects that move apart are said to repel. Objects that come together attract. Learners are only describing the pattern here, not explaining it.
quiz.placement: Station 4, Two balloons: rubbed balloons hung from threads push apart

quiz.prompt: Amina says a rubbed balloon hardly sticks to the wall at her home in Mombasa on a humid day (about 80% humidity). In Nairobi's dry season (about 35% humidity) a balloon sticks for about 3 minutes. Which statement is supported by this information?
choices: The balloon effect is the same on humid and dry days.
The balloon effect is stronger on humid days than on dry days.
The balloon effect is weaker on humid days than on dry days.
The balloon effect only works at the coast.
quiz.rationale: On the humid Mombasa day the balloon sticks for under 30 seconds or not at all. In dry Nairobi it sticks for about 3 minutes. So the effect is weaker when it is humid.
quiz.placement: Mr Mwangi shows the humid-day (Mombasa) and dry-season (Nairobi) data

quiz.prompt: Learners compare a rubbed balloon with a magnet. Which observation shows a difference between them?
choices: The rubbed balloon pulls things towards it from a short distance.
The rubbed balloon pulls on hair without touching it.
The rubbed balloon can pull on small pieces of paper, which are not metal.
The rubbed balloon can pull on things across a small gap of air.
quiz.rationale: A magnet needs a magnetic material such as iron to pull on, but the balloon pulls on paper pieces. Pulling without touching is a similarity, not a difference.
quiz.placement: Comparing the balloon with a magnet: what is the same and what is different

quiz.prompt: Kipchoge asks, 'Is the shock I feel from my woollen jersey like lightning?' At this point in the unit, what is the best way for the class to treat his question?
choices: Say the shock is only in his imagination.
Say the shock is caused by magnetism.
Write it on the Driving Question Board as a question to investigate in later lessons, since it has not been explained yet.
Answer that it is exactly the same as lightning, so the class can move on.
quiz.rationale: This is the opening lesson and the phenomenon is deliberately left unexplained. Good questions go on the DQB and are answered with evidence in later lessons.
quiz.placement: Building the Driving Question Board: Kipchoge's question about the shock and lightning

quiz.prompt: Learners draw an Initial Model of the balloon, hair, wall and paper. Which is the best thing to include in the model?
choices: Only the things they can see, with no arrows.
Nothing until the teacher tells them the right answer.
Only the correct textbook explanation, copied from a book.
Arrows and labels for anything they think moves or acts, even if they cannot name it yet.
quiz.rationale: An initial model shows what learners currently think is happening, including invisible things. It is a starting point that will be revised in later lessons, so there are no wrong models today.
quiz.placement: Initial Model drawing of balloon, hair, wall and paper piece

lessons.title: What Are Electric Charges? Atoms, Protons, Electrons and the Rule of Attraction and Repulsion

quiz.prompt: Two identical polythene strips are each rubbed 20 times with wool. One hangs from a thread and the other is brought near it without touching. What happens?
choices: The hanging strip is pushed away (they repel)
The strips attract because rubbed plastic becomes magnetic
Nothing happens because the strips are identical
The hanging strip is pulled towards the other strip (they attract)
quiz.rationale: Both strips are rubbed in the same way so they carry the same type of charge. Like charges repel, as the class table showed for two polythene strips.
quiz.placement: Part A: rods-and-strips investigation, step 1 (two polythene strips rubbed with wool/fur)

quiz.prompt: A polythene strip rubbed with wool hangs from a thread. A perspex rod rubbed with silk is brought near it. The strip moves towards the rod. What does this result support?
choices: Neutral objects always repel charged ones
Unlike charges attract
Only perspex can attract objects
Like charges attract
quiz.rationale: Polythene rubbed with wool/fur is negative and perspex rubbed with silk is positive. Their attraction shows that unlike charges attract.
quiz.placement: Part A: rods-and-strips investigation, step 3 (silk-rubbed perspex rod near hanging polythene strip)

quiz.prompt: One unrubbed polythene strip hangs from a thread. A second unrubbed polythene strip is brought near it. Nothing happens. Why was this control trial included?
choices: It shows that the push or pull seen earlier needs the strips to be rubbed (charged)
It shows that the strips only repel when they touch
It shows that thread stops all forces
It shows that polythene never carries charge
quiz.rationale: Unrubbed strips are not charged and show no effect. This shows the pushing and pulling in the other trials came from the charge produced by rubbing.
quiz.placement: Part A: rods-and-strips investigation, step 4 (unrubbed control strips)

quiz.prompt: An atom is made of protons, neutrons and electrons. Which statement about the charge of a neutron is correct?
choices: A neutron has a charge of -1.6 x 10^-19 C
A neutron has a very small positive charge
A neutron has a charge of 0 C (no charge)
A neutron has a charge of +1.6 x 10^-19 C
quiz.rationale: From the charge table, the proton is +1.6 x 10^-19 C, the electron is -1.6 x 10^-19 C and the neutron has no charge (0 C).
quiz.placement: Part B: 'Inside the Atom' card set and charge table

quiz.prompt: An atom has 3 protons and 2 electrons. A proton has a charge of +1.6 x 10^-19 C and an electron has a charge of -1.6 x 10^-19 C. What is the total charge of the atom?
choices: 0 C
quiz.rationale: Protons give 3 x (+1.6 x 10^-19) and electrons give 2 x (-1.6 x 10^-19). The total is (3 - 2) x 1.6 x 10^-19 = +1.6 x 10^-19 C, so the atom is not neutral.
quiz.placement: Part B: card sort building a neutral atom and a second atom with 3 protons and 2 electrons

quiz.prompt: In Lesson 1, two balloons were each rubbed on hair and hung on separate threads, and they pushed apart. What does this tell us about the charges on the two balloons?
choices: They carry opposite types of charge
One is charged and the other is neutral
Neither balloon is charged; the air pushes them apart
They carry the same type of charge
quiz.rationale: Objects that repel carry the same type of charge, because like charges repel and unlike charges attract. Both balloons were rubbed in the same way.
quiz.placement: Claim-evidence-reasoning poster, question 3 (applying the rule to the two balloons)

quiz.prompt: An ordinary piece of rubber contains protons (positive) and electrons (negative). Why does it not push or pull on everything around it all the time?
choices: It contains only neutrons, which are uncharged
Its protons and electrons are equal in number, so their charges cancel and it is neutral overall
Its electrons are held in the nucleus where they cannot act
It has no charged particles inside it
quiz.rationale: A normal atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons of equal size but opposite charge. The charges cancel, but the charged particles are still inside the atom.
quiz.placement: Claim-evidence-reasoning poster, question 2 (why a normal atom is neutral) and gallery walk discussion

quiz.prompt: You draw a model of a neutral atom in the balloon rubber. Which drawing is correct?
choices: Protons and neutrons in the nucleus, with electrons around it and equal numbers of + and - charges
Protons and electrons together in the nucleus, with neutrons around it
Protons and neutrons in the nucleus, with twice as many electrons as protons around it
Electrons in the nucleus and protons around it, with equal numbers of + and - charges
quiz.rationale: The nucleus holds protons (+) and neutrons (0) and the electrons (-) are outside it. A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons.
quiz.placement: Model revision 2: zoomed-in atoms in the balloon rubber and hair strand

lessons.title: Charging by Friction: Who Wins the Electrons?

quiz.prompt: On a dry Nairobi morning, Wanjiru combs her hair and her hair rises towards the comb. The comb and her hair were charged by rubbing against each other. What can you say about the charges on the comb and the hair?
choices: They have the same sign, because they were rubbed together
Only the comb is charged and the hair stays neutral
They have opposite signs, because the hair is attracted to the comb
Neither is charged, because rubbing only makes things warm
quiz.rationale: Unlike charges attract. Friction gives the two rubbed materials equal and opposite charges, so the hair is attracted to the comb.
quiz.placement: Predict: Wanjiru's comb and hair prediction (same or opposite charge)

quiz.prompt: A polythene strip, known to be negatively charged, hangs on a thread. A learner brings a rubbed rod close to it. Which result is reliable proof that the rod is negatively charged?
choices: The strip is repelled by the rod
The strip does not move at all
The strip is attracted to the rod
The strip swings towards the rod and then hangs still
quiz.rationale: Only repulsion proves the sign of charge, because like charges repel. Attraction could also happen with a neutral object or an oppositely charged one.
quiz.placement: Observe, Station B (Pairs): testing each rubbed object against the polythene and perspex references

quiz.prompt: This is the triboelectric order from most positive to most negative: dry human hair (+), glass, perspex, wool/fur, silk, polythene, ebonite, latex balloon (-). A glass rod is rubbed with a piece of silk. What charges do they gain?
choices: Glass becomes positive and silk becomes negative
Glass becomes negative and silk becomes positive
Both stay neutral because they are different materials
Both become positive
quiz.rationale: The material higher in the list becomes positive when rubbed with one lower in the list. Glass is higher than silk, so glass loses electrons and becomes positive, and silk gains them and becomes negative.
quiz.placement: Observe: comparing the class order with the triboelectric table (glass with silk pair)

quiz.prompt: A balloon is rubbed on dry hair. The balloon becomes negative and the hair becomes positive. What happened during the rubbing?
choices: Positive charges moved from the balloon to the hair
Electrons moved from the hair to the balloon
Electrons were created on the balloon by the rubbing
Protons moved from the balloon to the hair
quiz.rationale: In a solid only electrons move, because protons are fixed in the nucleus. The balloon gains extra electrons and is negative, and the hair has a deficit of electrons and is positive.
quiz.placement: Explain, Steps 1-2: particle-level diagram of electron transfer between hair and balloon

quiz.prompt: A balloon is rubbed on dry hair and gains 6 × 10^9 extra electrons. What is true about the hair and the total charge?
choices: The hair loses 6 × 10^9 electrons, so the hair is positive and the total charge stays zero
The hair also gains 6 × 10^9 electrons, so both become negative
The hair loses 6 × 10^9 protons, so the hair is positive
The hair stays neutral, because the balloon made its own charge
quiz.rationale: Charge is transferred, not created. The electrons the balloon gains come from the hair, so the hair has an equal and opposite charge and the total charge stays zero.
quiz.placement: Explain, Step 3: charge conservation (6 electrons moved: balloon -6, hair +6, total 0)

quiz.prompt: A rubbed balloon gains a charge of 2 nC (2 × 10^-9 C). One electron has a charge of 1.6 × 10^-19 C. About how many extra electrons did the balloon gain?
quiz.rationale: Number of electrons = total charge ÷ charge of one electron = 2 × 10^-9 ÷ 1.6 × 10^-19 = 1.25 × 10^10. This is still a tiny fraction of the roughly 10^23 atoms in a balloon.
quiz.placement: Explain, Step 4: calculation of the number of electrons for 1 nC, then 2 nC

quiz.prompt: A balloon rubbed on hair sticks to a classroom wall. The wall was never rubbed. Why can rubbing alone NOT explain why the balloon sticks to the wall?
choices: The wall was not rubbed, so a different explanation is needed for its attraction
Friction between balloon and hair made the wall positive
The wall has protons that move towards the balloon
The wall gained electrons from the balloon by friction
quiz.rationale: Charging by friction explains why the balloon and hair become charged. The wall was not rubbed, so its attraction to the balloon needs another explanation, which the class will meet in a later lesson.
quiz.placement: DQB: new question 'Why does the balloon stick to the neutral wall?'

lessons.title: Conductors and Insulators: Why Does the Balloon Keep Its Charge While a Metal Spoon Does Not?

quiz.prompt: In a circuit with two 1.5 V cells in series (3 V) and a torch bulb, a learner touches each material to the gap in turn. Which list contains ONLY materials that made the bulb light?
choices: Aluminium foil, dry wood, glass rod, graphite
Copper wire, aluminium foil, steel spoon, graphite
Steel spoon, rubber, copper wire, dry cotton cloth
Copper wire, plastic ruler, steel spoon, graphite
quiz.rationale: Copper, aluminium, steel and graphite are conductors, so the bulb lights. Plastic, dry wood, rubber, glass and dry cotton are insulators, so the bulb stays off.
quiz.placement: Observe: groups of 4 test the 9 materials in the simple 3 V circuit and record Lit or Not lit

quiz.prompt: A group touches the two bare wire ends of their circuit together and the bulb lights. They then place a dry wooden stick across the gap and the bulb does NOT light. What is the best conclusion?
choices: The cell has gone flat
Dry wood is an insulator, so electrons cannot move through it
Wood has no electrons in it
The circuit is broken, so nothing can be learned about wood
quiz.rationale: The bulb lit when the wires touched, so the circuit and cell work. The bulb stayed off with wood because its electrons are tightly bound and cannot move through it. Wood does have electrons.
quiz.placement: Observe: teacher asks 'Is the circuit broken, or is the material not letting electrons pass?' and groups test the bulb first

quiz.prompt: Graphite (pencil lead) is not a metal, yet the bulb lights when graphite is placed in the gap of the circuit. What does this result tell us?
choices: Pencil lead is secretly a metal
Graphite has free electrons that can move, so metals are not the only conductors
The bulb was lit by the wood around the pencil lead
Graphite has free protons that carry the electricity
quiz.rationale: The bulb lit, so graphite has free (delocalised) electrons. This shows that the rule 'only metals conduct' is not enough, and we need the idea of free electrons.
quiz.placement: Observe: prompt 'Which result surprised your group? Is graphite a metal?'

quiz.prompt: What is different about the electrons in a copper wire and in a plastic ruler?
choices: Copper has free electrons that can move through it, but plastic's electrons are tightly bound to their atoms
Copper has electrons but plastic has none
Copper's electrons are positive and plastic's are negative
Plastic has more electrons, so they cannot move
quiz.rationale: Both materials contain electrons. In copper some are free (delocalised) and drift through the metal, but in plastic they are tightly bound and cannot move through the material.
quiz.placement: Explain: sorting the 9 materials and drawing free versus bound electrons in a conductor and an insulator

quiz.prompt: Why do we say a conductor has free electrons and not free protons?
choices: Protons are too small to move
In solids the protons stay fixed in the nucleus, so only electrons can move
Protons are free in metals, but electrons are free in insulators
Protons are negatively charged, so they are repelled by the cell
quiz.rationale: Protons are held in the nucleus of each atom, so in a solid only electrons move. Protons are positively charged, not negatively charged.
quiz.placement: Explain: teacher says 'Only electrons move in solids; protons stay in the nucleus' and asks why we say free electrons, not free protons

quiz.prompt: A latex balloon is rubbed on hair and gains extra electrons. It then stays charged and stuck to a wall for about 3 minutes on a dry day. Which explanation is correct?
choices: The wall keeps giving the balloon new electrons all the time
Latex is an insulator, so the extra electrons cannot move through it and stay where they were deposited
Latex is a conductor, so the electrons stay trapped inside the balloon
The electrons are used up as soon as the balloon touches the wall, so the charge must be made again
quiz.rationale: Latex rubber is an insulator, as the bulb test showed. Its electrons are bound, so the extra electrons cannot spread through the balloon and the charge stays in place.
quiz.placement: Explain: applying the idea to the balloon ('Why does the extra charge on the rubbed balloon stay on the balloon?')

quiz.prompt: A group predicted that a glass rod would light the bulb, but the bulb stayed off. The group retested it once with firm contacts and got the same result. What should they do next?
choices: Record 'Not lit' honestly and mark glass as an insulator
Leave the result blank because it was a surprise
Record 'Lit' because glass is a solid like metals
Change the recorded result to 'Lit' so it matches their prediction
quiz.rationale: Good investigators record what they observe, even when it surprises them. The retest confirmed the result, so glass is recorded as not lit and classed as an insulator.
quiz.placement: Observe: groups compare results with their predictions and retest any 'odd' result once

quiz.prompt: A balloon is rubbed on hair, and electrons move from the hair to the balloon. Which description should be in the revised particle model?
choices: Both the balloon and the hair are neutral because charge is destroyed by rubbing
The balloon is negative because it gained electrons, and the hair is positive because it lost electrons
The balloon is positive because it gained protons, and the hair is negative
The balloon is negative because positive charges moved from the balloon to the hair
quiz.rationale: Only electrons move in solids. The balloon gains electrons and becomes negative, and the hair loses electrons and becomes positive. Charge is moved, not created or destroyed.
quiz.placement: Model: learners revise their particle-level model of the balloon, hair, wall and paper in a different colour

lessons.title: Charging by Contact: Why Do Paper Pieces Touch the Balloon and Then Fall Off?

quiz.prompt: A neutral gold-leaf electroscope has its leaf hanging straight down. A polythene strip rubbed with wool (so it is negative) is touched to the metal cap and then taken away. What will the leaf do after the strip is removed?
choices: It stays raised, because charge has moved onto the electroscope
It goes even higher once the strip is removed
It stays down the whole time because polythene is an insulator
It falls straight back down as soon as the strip is removed
quiz.rationale: Touching lets electrons move from the strip onto the metal cap, stem and leaf. The electroscope keeps this charge after the strip is removed, so the leaf stays diverged.
quiz.placement: Predict: learners sketch the leaf before, during and after touching the negative strip to the cap

quiz.prompt: A neutral electroscope has a negative polythene strip held close to its cap but NOT touching it. The leaf rises. The strip is then taken away. What does the leaf do, and why?
choices: It falls back down, because no charge was transferred to the electroscope
It rises higher, because the strip is now further away
It stays raised, because the strip left its charge behind
It falls back down, because the strip's charge was used up
quiz.rationale: With no contact, no electrons were transferred, so the electroscope is still neutral overall. When the strip is removed the leaf falls back. Only contact leaves the leaf raised.
quiz.placement: Observe: bring the rubbed strip near the cap without touching, then take it away

quiz.prompt: A electroscope has been charged by touching it with a negative polythene strip, and its leaf is raised. A learner then touches the metal cap with a finger. What do they see, and what does it show?
choices: The leaf collapses, because the extra charge is conducted away through the finger
The leaf stays the same, because the charge is trapped on the leaf
The leaf rises higher, because the finger adds more charge
The leaf rises and falls repeatedly, because the finger is neutral
quiz.rationale: The body can conduct the extra electrons away from the electroscope. With no excess charge left, the leaf hangs down again. This is how the class discharged the electroscope between trials.
quiz.placement: Observe: step 4, discharging the electroscope by touching the cap with a finger

quiz.prompt: A negative polythene strip touches the metal cap of a neutral electroscope. Which statement correctly describes what moves?
choices: Positive charges move from the strip onto the cap
Electrons move from the strip onto the cap and spread down the stem to the leaf
Protons move from the electroscope onto the strip
Electrons are created in the cap by the touch of the strip
quiz.rationale: In a solid only electrons move. The strip has extra electrons, and the metal has free electrons, so electrons move from the strip onto the metal and spread through the cap, stem and leaf. Charge is transferred, not created.
quiz.placement: Explain: question 2, what the free electrons do when the negative strip touches the metal cap

quiz.prompt: After a negative strip has touched a neutral electroscope and been removed, the leaf stays raised. What is the sign of the electroscope's charge, and why does the leaf rise?
choices: Positive, because the leaf lost electrons to the strip
Negative, because the stem and leaf attract the strip even though it has gone
Positive, because the stem and leaf attract each other
Negative, because the stem and leaf both have extra electrons and like charges repel
quiz.rationale: Contact gives the SAME sign as the charged object. The stem and leaf both gain extra electrons and become negative, and like charges repel, so the leaf rises.
quiz.placement: Explain: questions 3 and 4, why the leaf stays diverged and what sign the electroscope now has

quiz.prompt: A positive perspex rod touches the cap of a neutral electroscope. What sign of charge does the electroscope gain, and which way do electrons move?
choices: Positive; electrons move from the rod to the electroscope
Negative; electrons move from the rod to the electroscope
Negative; electrons move from the electroscope to the rod
Positive; electrons move from the electroscope to the rod
quiz.rationale: Contact gives the same sign, so the electroscope becomes positive. A positive rod has a shortage of electrons, so electrons move from the electroscope onto the rod, leaving the electroscope with a deficit.
quiz.placement: Explain: exit question about a positive perspex rod touching a neutral electroscope

quiz.prompt: A neutral paper piece jumps up to a negative balloon, touches it, and then falls off. Which explanation is correct?
choices: The paper piece lost electrons to the balloon, became positive and was repelled
The paper piece became magnetic after touching the balloon and was pushed away
The balloon's charge was used up when the paper touched it, so nothing held the paper
The paper piece gained some electrons from the balloon, became negative like the balloon, and was repelled
quiz.rationale: On contact a few electrons move from the negative balloon onto the paper. The paper then has the same sign as the balloon, and like charges repel, so it falls off.
quiz.placement: Model Building: revising the particle model with the paper piece touching the balloon and then being repelled

lessons.title: Charging by Induction and Earthing: Charging Without Touching

quiz.prompt: A balloon is rubbed on dry hair and becomes negative. It is held 2 cm above small pieces of neutral paper, and the pieces jump up to the balloon. Which explanation is correct?
choices: Electrons in the paper shift away from the balloon, leaving the near side of the paper positive, so it is attracted.
The balloon gives electrons to the paper before touching it, so the paper becomes negative.
The balloon is sticky, so it pulls the paper up.
The paper was already positively charged before the balloon arrived.
quiz.rationale: The negative balloon repels electrons in the neutral paper, leaving the side nearest the balloon positive. The balloon attracts this nearer positive side, and no charge needs to be added to the paper.
quiz.placement: Predict: Mr Mwangi holds a rubbed balloon 2 cm above torn paper pieces and learners predict why a neutral paper jumps

quiz.prompt: A neutral gold-leaf electroscope has its leaf hanging down. A rubbed polythene strip (negative) is brought near the cap without touching it, and the leaf diverges. When the strip is taken away, the leaf falls back down. What does this show?
choices: The strip lost all its charge when it was brought near the cap.
The electroscope lost protons while the strip was near and got them back later.
The electroscope gained electrons from the strip and then lost them to the air.
No charge stayed on the electroscope. Its electrons only moved within the metal and then spread back.
quiz.rationale: The strip never touched the cap, so no charge was transferred. The electrons moved down to the leaf while the strip was near, then spread back when it was removed, and the total charge stayed zero.
quiz.placement: Station 2: Induction on the electroscope (strip near the cap, then removed)

quiz.prompt: A negative polythene strip is held near the cap of a gold-leaf electroscope, and the leaf diverges. With the strip still near, a learner touches the cap with a finger and the leaf collapses. What has happened?
choices: Electrons have been repelled through the finger to the Earth, leaving the electroscope with a deficit of electrons.
Protons have moved from the electroscope through the finger to the Earth.
The finger has neutralised the charge on the polythene strip.
Electrons have flowed from the Earth through the finger onto the electroscope, making it more negative.
quiz.rationale: The negative strip repels the free electrons away from the cap, and with the finger touching they escape to the Earth. Less negative charge on the leaf means the leaf collapses.
quiz.placement: Station 3: Charging by induction with earthing, Step 2 (touch the cap with a finger)

quiz.prompt: In charging by induction, the finger must be removed from the cap BEFORE the negative strip is taken away. Why?
choices: If the strip were removed first, electrons would flow back from the Earth and the electroscope would end up neutral.
The strip would lose its charge if it were taken away while the finger touched the cap.
The finger would become charged and give the learner a shock.
Removing the strip first would give the electroscope the same sign as the strip.
quiz.rationale: While the finger touches the cap, the electroscope is connected to the Earth. If the strip leaves first, electrons would flow back in from the Earth and cancel the deficit, so no charge would be left.
quiz.placement: Explain Task 2: Earthing and the opposite sign (why the order of finger off first matters)

quiz.prompt: A neutral electroscope is charged by induction using a negative strip and earthing, following the steps: strip near, finger touches the cap, finger removed, strip removed. The leaf then stays diverged. What is the charge on the electroscope?
choices: Positive, the opposite sign to the strip, because it has a deficit of electrons.
Negative, the same sign as the strip, because the strip transferred electrons to it.
Neutral, because the strip never touched the cap.
Negative, because electrons came from the Earth through the finger.
quiz.rationale: Electrons were pushed to the Earth while the strip was near. The electroscope is left with a deficit of electrons, so it is positive, the opposite of the strip.
quiz.placement: Explain Task 2: Earthing and the opposite sign (sign of the electroscope after Step 4)

quiz.prompt: Which statement correctly compares charging by contact and charging by induction with earthing?
choices: Both give the same sign, but induction needs earthing.
Contact gives the same sign as the charged object, while induction with earthing gives the opposite sign.
Both give the opposite sign, but contact needs the objects to touch.
Contact gives the opposite sign and induction gives the same sign as the charged object.
quiz.rationale: In contact, electrons are shared with the touching object, so it takes the same sign. In induction, the charged object never touches and earthing removes or adds electrons, leaving the opposite sign.
quiz.placement: Explain Task 3: Contrast with contact (three-column comparison of contact, induction and separation)

quiz.prompt: A negative balloon is brought near a neutral piece of paper. The near side of the paper becomes positive and the far side becomes negative. Why is the paper pulled towards the balloon and not pushed away?
choices: The far side of the paper has no charge, so only attraction acts.
The positive charges on the paper are larger than the negative charges.
The paper gains extra electrons from the balloon and becomes positive overall.
The positive side is nearer to the balloon, so the attraction is stronger than the repulsion from the farther negative side.
quiz.rationale: The electric force is stronger when charges are closer. The nearer positive side is attracted more strongly than the farther negative side is repelled, so there is a net attraction. The total charge of the paper is still zero.
quiz.placement: Explain Task 4: Back to the phenomenon (wall and paper, attraction stronger than repulsion)

quiz.prompt: On a dry day in Nairobi, a rubbed balloon sticks to a painted wall for several minutes. In Mombasa during the rainy season, the same balloon falls off the wall quickly. What is the best explanation?
choices: The balloon is heavier in humid air, so it falls.
Rain makes the wall conduct electricity, so the wall repels the balloon.
Water vapour in the air lets charge leak away from the balloon, so there is less charge to separate charge in the wall.
The humid air adds protons to the balloon, making it neutral.
quiz.rationale: Moist air lets the balloon's charge leak away. With less charge on the balloon, it causes less charge separation in the wall, so the attraction is too weak to hold it.
quiz.placement: Model Building: note on the effect of humidity (balloon falls quickly in Mombasa)

quiz.prompt: A learner asks: 'Where do the charges in the neutral paper come from when the balloon makes it jump?' Which answer is correct?
choices: The charges were in the paper all along. Electrons only moved a little, so no charge was created.
The air gives the paper new positive charges.
The paper makes extra electrons when it is attracted.
The balloon creates new charges in the paper as it comes near.
quiz.rationale: Paper is made of atoms with both positive and negative charges, so a neutral piece already has charge. The balloon only makes the electrons shift, and charge is conserved.
quiz.placement: Driving Question Board: answering 'Why is paper attracted to the balloon if it is neutral?' and 'Where do the charges in the paper come from?'

lessons.title: Distribution of Charge on Conductors: Outer Surfaces, Points, Sparks and Lightning Conductors

quiz.prompt: A hollow metal can on an insulating stand is given a negative charge. A proof plane touched on the OUTSIDE of the can and then on the cap of a gold-leaf electroscope makes the leaves diverge clearly. Where do the extra electrons sit on the can?
choices: Only at the bottom of the can
On the inner surface of the can
Evenly spread through the inside of the metal
On the outer surface of the can
quiz.rationale: Free electrons in a conductor repel each other and move as far apart as possible, so they collect on the outer surface. The clear leaf divergence from the outside is the evidence.
quiz.placement: Predict: drawing where extra electrons sit on the hollow can and the pear-shaped conductor

quiz.prompt: Why do the extra electrons on a charged metal conductor move apart to the outside?
choices: The positive charges in the metal pull the electrons outwards
Electrons are heavier than the metal atoms, so they sink to the surface
The air outside the metal attracts the electrons
Electrons repel each other (like charges repel) and are free to move in a conductor
quiz.rationale: Metals have free electrons. Like charges repel, so the electrons push each other as far apart as possible, which is the outer surface.
quiz.placement: Predict: one-sentence reason using free electrons and like charges repelling

quiz.prompt: After the can is charged negatively, a proof plane touched on the INSIDE of the can is moved to a gold-leaf electroscope and the leaves hardly diverge. What is the correct conclusion?
choices: The electroscope is faulty because the can is charged
There are no electrons inside the metal of the can
There is little or no charge on the inside surface, but the can is still charged
The can is not charged at all
quiz.rationale: The proof plane collects almost no charge from the inside because the extra charge sits on the outer surface. The can is still charged, and the electrons are on the outside.
quiz.placement: Part A: proof plane on the inside of the can, then the electroscope

quiz.prompt: A charged pear-shaped metal conductor is tested with a proof plane and an electroscope. The pointed end makes the leaves diverge strongly and the flat end makes them diverge only slightly. What does this show?
choices: Charge is more concentrated at the pointed end
The flat end has more charge than the pointed end
The charge is spread evenly over the whole conductor
Charge is created at the pointed end
quiz.rationale: Greater leaf divergence means the proof plane collected more charge, so charge is concentrated at the point, where electrons crowd closer together.
quiz.placement: Part B: pear-shaped conductor, pointed end and flat end

quiz.prompt: Before each new reading with the same electroscope, the teacher touches the cap with a finger so the leaves fall together. Why is this done?
choices: To give the electroscope extra charge
To earth the electroscope and remove the charge left from the previous test
To cool the metal cap
To make the leaves more sensitive by adding positive charge
quiz.rationale: Touching with a finger earths the electroscope, so the leaves fall together and each new reading starts with no charge.
quiz.placement: Part A and Part B: earthing the electroscope between tests

quiz.prompt: At a sharply pointed part of a charged conductor, the electric field is so strong that it ionises the air and charge leaks away. What is this process called?
choices: Electrostatic shielding
Earthing by friction
Point discharge
Induction
quiz.rationale: Point discharge is the leaking of charge into the air from a point, where the field is strongest. It explains sparks and the action of lightning conductors.
quiz.placement: Explain: introducing point discharge

quiz.prompt: A lightning conductor on a building in Kericho has a pointed metal rod on top, joined by thick copper strip to a metal plate buried in the ground. Why is the top of the rod pointed?
choices: Points create extra electrons to cancel the lightning
Points attract more lightning than flat plates
Charge leaks away gradually from a point (point discharge)
Points stop the copper strip from rusting
quiz.rationale: A point has strong charge concentration, so charge leaks away into the air gradually. If lightning strikes, the rod and copper give a safe path to earth.
quiz.placement: Explain: lightning conductor in Kericho (pointed rod, copper strip, earth plate)

quiz.prompt: Kipchoge asks if the shock from a woollen jersey on a dry Nairobi day is like lightning. Which answer is best?
choices: No, a jersey shock involves protons moving, while lightning involves electrons
No, the shock is magnetic and lightning is electrical
Yes, because both are caused by static electricity creating new charges
Yes, both are discharges of charge, but lightning is much larger
quiz.rationale: Both are electrostatic discharges where built-up charge moves. Lightning is a much larger discharge. Charge is transferred, not created.
quiz.placement: Explain: comparing the lightning conductor with Kipchoge's question

quiz.prompt: On a student's particle-level model of a charged metal object touched by a balloon, which drawing is correct?
choices: Electrons spread on the outer surface, closer together at any pointed part
Electrons spread evenly through the inside of the metal
Electrons all collected at the flat part of the object
Positive charges moving along the surface
quiz.rationale: On a conductor the extra electrons sit on the outer surface and crowd closer together at points. In solids only electrons move.
quiz.placement: Model: revising the particle-level diagram of the balloon, hair, wall and paper

lessons.title: Detecting and Measuring Charge: The Gold-Leaf Electroscope

quiz.prompt: A gold-leaf electroscope has an insulating stopper where the metal rod passes into the case. What is the main job of this insulating stopper?
choices: It makes the leaf heavy so it hangs down
It carries electrons from the leaf to the Earth
It collects charge from the charged object
It stops charge leaking away from the cap, stem and leaf
quiz.rationale: The stopper and case are insulators, so charge stays on the metal cap, stem and leaf instead of leaking away. The cap collects charge and the metal stem and leaf let it spread.
quiz.placement: Predict: naming the parts of the electroscope (cap, stem, leaf, insulating stopper) and their jobs

quiz.prompt: A rubbed polythene strip (negative) is brought near the cap of a neutral electroscope without touching it. The leaf lifts away from the stem. Which explanation is correct?
choices: The strip gives the leaf a positive charge, so it is pulled upward
Electrons are pushed down the stem to the leaf, so the leaf and stem both have excess electrons and repel
The leaf is attracted to the strip because the strip is magnetic
Protons in the cap move down the stem into the leaf
quiz.rationale: The negative strip repels electrons in the metal down the stem to the leaf. The leaf and stem then have the same (negative) charge and like charges repel, so the leaf diverges.
quiz.placement: Explain: particle-level diagram of the electroscope when the negative strip is near the cap

quiz.prompt: A negatively charged polythene strip touches the cap of an electroscope and is then taken away. The leaf stays diverged. Why does it stay diverged?
choices: The strip is still pulling the leaf upward from a distance
Protons moved from the strip onto the electroscope and are stuck there
The leaf is stuck to the stem and cannot fall
Electrons moved from the strip to the electroscope, so the leaf and stem keep excess electrons and repel
quiz.rationale: On contact, electrons pass from the strip to the electroscope. They stay on the leaf and stem, so repulsion continues after the strip is removed. The strip cannot be pulling the leaf because it is no longer there.
quiz.placement: Observe: Step 3, touch the strip to the cap (contact), remove the strip and record what the leaf does

quiz.prompt: The same electroscope is charged by contact with a polythene strip rubbed 20 strokes, and the leaf diverges. After it is discharged, it is charged again with a strip rubbed 40 strokes and the leaf diverges more. What does this show?
choices: The leaf diverges more only because the strip is longer
The electroscope has become more sensitive after the first test
More strokes make the leaf lighter
More charge on the leaf and stem gives more repulsion and a bigger divergence
quiz.rationale: On the same electroscope, more strokes put more charge on the leaf and stem, so repulsion and divergence are greater. Divergence shows the amount of charge.
quiz.placement: Observe: Step 6, repeat the contact charging with 40 strokes and compare with 20 strokes

quiz.prompt: An electroscope is charged negatively and its leaf is diverged. A rubbed object is brought near the cap without touching it, and the leaf diverges less. What does this show about the charge on the object?
choices: It is neutral, so it has no effect on the leaf
It has a negative charge, the same as the electroscope
It has the opposite (positive) charge to the electroscope
Nothing can be known about its charge
quiz.rationale: A positive object attracts electrons up toward the cap, so the leaf and stem have fewer excess electrons and the divergence falls. A decrease in divergence means the opposite sign.
quiz.placement: Explain: sign test, with the perspex rod (positive) making the leaf diverge less

quiz.prompt: A negatively charged electroscope has its leaf diverged. A learner touches the cap with a finger and the leaf collapses. What happens?
choices: The finger adds more electrons, so the leaf repels more strongly
Electrons flow from the electroscope through the finger to the Earth, leaving it neutral, so the leaf collapses
Electrons stay on the leaf but the finger pushes the leaf down
Protons flow from the Earth into the electroscope, so the leaf falls
quiz.rationale: Earthing lets the excess electrons flow through the finger to the Earth. With no excess charge on the leaf and stem there is no repulsion, so the leaf falls.
quiz.placement: Explain: earthing, electrons flowing to the Earth through the finger

quiz.prompt: Amina rubs a balloon 20 strokes on dry hair and brings it near the cap of a neutral electroscope without touching it. The leaf rises. What can she correctly conclude from this alone?
choices: The balloon is magnetic
The balloon is positively charged
The balloon is charged, but the rise alone does not show its sign
The balloon is negatively charged for certain
quiz.rationale: A leaf rising on a neutral electroscope shows only that the object is charged. The sign needs a sign test on an already charged electroscope.
quiz.placement: Model Building: adding the 'How do we know?' detector box showing the electroscope near the negative balloon

quiz.prompt: On a humid day in Mombasa, a charged electroscope's leaf slowly falls even though nobody touches the cap. What is the best explanation?
choices: The electrons turn into protons in humid air
Charge leaks away through the damp air, so repulsion becomes weaker
The leaf has become heavier because it has absorbed protons
The Earth pulls harder on the leaf in humid places
quiz.rationale: Damp air lets charge escape from the electroscope. With less charge on the leaf and stem there is less repulsion, so the leaf collapses. This links to Amina's balloon question about her coastal home.
quiz.placement: Driving Question Board: Amina's Mombasa question and testing the humidity idea with the electroscope

lessons.title: Applications and Consolidation: From the Mysterious Balloon to Lightning Conductors, and the Final Explanation

quiz.prompt: A school in Kericho has a lightning conductor: a pointed metal rod on the roof joined by a thick copper strip to a metal plate buried in the ground. Which statement best explains how it protects the building?
choices: The pointed rod is magnetic, so it pulls lightning away from the roof and into the sky
Charge crowds at the sharp point and leaks gradually into the air, and the copper strip lets electrons flow safely to or from the ground
The copper strip is an insulator that stops electrons from reaching the building
The rod stores all the charge from the storm so that the building stays neutral
quiz.rationale: Charge crowds at a sharp point, so charge leaks away through the air gradually. The thick copper strip and earth plate give electrons a safe path to or from the ground. It does not attract lightning by magnetism.
quiz.placement: Station 1: Lightning conductor (Kericho and Kisumu), and the CER explanation for the lightning conductor

quiz.prompt: A fuel tanker at a Nairobi petrol depot trails a metal chain on the ground. Fuel rubbing on the pipe wall can charge the tank. Why is the chain used?
choices: It cools the fuel so that less vapour is produced
It stops the fuel from rubbing on the pipe wall, so no charge forms at all
It lets electrons flow to the ground, so charge cannot build up on the tank and cause a spark near fuel vapour
It adds extra positive charge to the tank so that the tank becomes neutral
quiz.rationale: The chain earths the tanker. Electrons flow to the ground, so friction charge cannot build up and no spark can ignite the fuel vapour. The chain does not stop the rubbing; it removes the charge that rubbing produces.
quiz.placement: Station 2: Fuel tanker at a Nairobi petrol depot, and the CER explanation for the fuel tanker

quiz.prompt: In an electrostatic precipitator at a cement factory, smoke dust particles are given a negative charge as they rise up the chimney. The dust is then collected on metal plates. What charge must the plates carry to collect the dust?
choices: No charge at all, because dust falls onto plates by gravity only
Positive, because unlike charges attract
Negative, because like charges attract
Either sign, because the sign of the plate does not affect the dust
quiz.rationale: Unlike charges attract. Negatively charged dust is pulled to positively charged plates. Plates with the same negative charge would repel the dust.
quiz.placement: Station 4: Electrostatic precipitator at Athi River

quiz.prompt: A photocopier drum attracts toner powder that has the opposite charge to the drum. A learner says the same idea can be seen when a rubbed polythene strip is passed over small paper pieces. What do the paper pieces do?
choices: They jump up and stick to the strip, because the charged strip attracts the neutral paper
They jump up only if the strip is wet
They are not affected, because paper is an insulator and cannot be attracted
They are pushed away, because the strip and the paper have the same charge
quiz.rationale: The charged strip makes the near side of each neutral paper piece oppositely charged (induction), so the attraction is stronger than the repulsion. The pieces jump and stick, as toner does on the drum. Keeping the strip dry matters, because moisture lets charge leak away.
quiz.placement: Station 3: Photocopier, dry demonstration with a rubbed polythene strip and paper pieces

quiz.prompt: In a spray gun used to paint a metal gate, all the paint droplets are given the same sign of charge. What is the effect of this?
choices: The droplets can only coat the side of the gate that faces the gun
The droplets repel each other and spread into a fine, even mist
The droplets attract each other and join into large drops
The droplets become neutral as they leave the gun
quiz.rationale: Droplets with the same sign of charge repel one another, so they spread out into a fine mist. The gate is earthed or oppositely charged, so the droplets are attracted to it and coat it evenly.
quiz.placement: Guided research worksheet: Card A, spray gun

quiz.prompt: Kipchoge feels a small shock after removing a woollen jersey in Nairobi. He asks if it is like lightning. Which answer is correct?
choices: No, lightning is caused by electrons but the jersey shock is caused by positive charge moving
Yes, and both involve the same amount of charge
Yes, both are discharges of built-up charge, but lightning involves vastly more charge
No, the jersey shock is caused by magnetism, but lightning is caused by charge
quiz.rationale: Both are the sudden discharge of charge built up by friction and transferred as electrons. The difference is the amount of charge: the jersey shock involves a tiny charge, like the balloon's about 1 nC, while lightning involves vastly more.
quiz.placement: Explain phase: Kipchoge's question, how the jersey shock is like and unlike lightning

quiz.prompt: At Amina's home in Mombasa, a rubbed balloon sticks to the wall for under 30 seconds or not at all when the relative humidity is about 80%. In Nairobi, at about 35% relative humidity, it sticks for about 3 minutes. What is the best explanation?
choices: Water vapour in humid air lets the charge on the balloon escape quickly
Friction cannot transfer electrons in warm places
Mombasa walls are always made of conductors
Balloons made in Mombasa carry less mass
quiz.rationale: At high humidity, water vapour in the air lets the charge leak away from the balloon quickly, so it loses its charge and falls. In dry air the charge stays much longer.
quiz.placement: Explain phase: 'Amina, why did the balloon fail at your coastal home?' and the balloon humidity data

quiz.prompt: A rubbed balloon sticks to a neutral wall. Which statement explains why the wall attracts the balloon?
choices: Neutral objects are repelled by charged objects, but the wall is held by static electricity
The wall is positively charged to begin with, so it attracts the negative balloon
The balloon is magnetic, and the wall contains iron
The negative balloon pushes electrons in the wall away from the near surface, leaving it positive, so the attraction is stronger than the repulsion
quiz.rationale: The negative balloon makes electrons in the wall shift away from the near surface (induction). The near surface becomes positive and is attracted to the balloon. This attraction is stronger than the repulsion from the far, negative side.
quiz.placement: Model phase: final particle-level model, part (4) wall and paper

quiz.prompt: A balloon is rubbed on hair. Electrons move from the hair to the balloon, and the balloon gains a charge of 1 nC (negative). What is true of the hair?
choices: The hair has a larger positive charge than the balloon's, because positive charges move in the hair
The hair has a positive charge of 1 nC, because charge is conserved
The hair has no charge, because charge is not created
The hair gains an extra negative charge of 1 nC
quiz.rationale: Charge is transferred, not created. Whatever electrons the balloon gains, the hair loses, so the hair ends up with an equal positive charge of 1 nC (a deficit of electrons). Total charge stays the same.
quiz.placement: Model phase: final particle-level model, part (2) after rubbing, and the Final Explanation on conservation of charge
